regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: CAPTEM combines two oral chemotherapy medicines to help control an advanced pancreatic NET. The team discusses the intended benefit, side effects and alternatives. NCCP identifies this pancreatic NET use as outside the medicines’ licences, requiring the local consent process.
regimen_profiles.treatment_setting: Locally advanced or metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour under NCCP 00505a.
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Capecitabine: Capecitabine is changed into fluorouracil, which interferes with the processes cells use to make and use their genetic instructions. This can damage cancer cells, but healthy bowel, mouth, skin and blood-forming cells can also be affected. Temozolomide: Temozolomide produces DNA damage that can prevent cancer cells from continuing to grow. Blood-forming cells and other healthy tissues can also be affected, so nausea prevention, blood counts, infection awareness and liver tests are important.
regimen_profiles.schedule_context: Each cycle lasts 28 days: capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14; add temozolomide once daily on Days 10–14; take neither anticancer medicine on Days 15–28. NCCP plans six cycles unless progression or unacceptable toxicity changes the plan.
key_points: Each cycle lasts 28 days: capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14; add temozolomide once daily on Days 10–14; take neither anticancer medicine on Days 15–28. NCCP plans six cycles unless progression or unacceptable toxicity changes the plan.

Before starting: blood count, kidney/liver tests, hepatitis B screening and DPD testing unless already tested. Blood count, kidney and liver tests before every cycle; liver tests also after each cycle. INR if indicated with warfarin. Liver injury can appear weeks after the last dose. Scans and hormone markers follow the consultant plan.
DPD testing before first capecitabine unless already tested; complete deficiency excludes use and partial deficiency needs individual dosing. Do not invent a fixed partial-DPD percentage.

Distinguish baseline capecitabine counts (NCCP caution versus EMA no-treatment wording at ANC<1.5 or platelets<100), unscheduled within-cycle capecitabine interruption (ANC<1 or platelets<75), and later combination recovery (ANC≥1.5 and platelets≥75).

Combination haematology uses both nadirs, recurrence and both previous doses. Printed rounded table bands have decimal gaps; no rounding into a safe band. Severe first-event stop versus reduced-dose continuation remains a specialist choice.

Capecitabine organ rules are not temozolomide rules. NCCP capecitabine CrCl 30–50 uses 75% of original, while the starting CAPTEM dose differs from EMA examples; reconcile explicitly. Severe renal impairment/dialysis must not be cleared because temozolomide may need no adjustment.
Treatment-related capecitabine bilirubin>3×ULN or ALT/AST>2.5×ULN requires interruption. The source recovery OR wording is ambiguous when another threshold remains high; keep the hold/review visible.
Severe hepatic exclusion conflicts with permissive table wording for components; source tension needs specialist review. Temozolomide liver injury can occur weeks after treatment.
Capecitabine grade 2/3 hand-foot syndrome requires a hold; the grade 3 subsequent reduction percentage is not supplied. Do not invent it.
Table dose percentages must not re-escalate prior toxicity reductions; omitted toxicity doses are not replaced.
Temozolomide Days 10–14 has oral moderate–high emetic risk. PJP prevention is local-risk-based; no automatic transfer of the glioma 42-day radiotherapy schedule.

premedication_and_prophylaxis: Capecitabine is minimal-to-low emetogenic, while temozolomide is moderate-to-high emetogenic in this oral schedule. The team must prescribe an oral anti-sickness plan for Days 10–14 and any rescue treatment; this is not a single low-risk infusion plan.

administration.cycle_and_sequence: Each cycle lasts 28 days: capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14; add temozolomide once daily on Days 10–14; take neither anticancer medicine on Days 15–28. NCCP plans six cycles unless progression or unacceptable toxicity changes the plan.
route_and_duration: The source starting schedule is capecitabine 750 mg/m² twice daily on Days 1–14 and temozolomide 200 mg/m² once daily on Days 10–14 of a 28-day cycle. Swallow both whole; do not crush, cut or open them.

Have the Days 10–14 anti-sickness prescription ready before Day 10. Ask how it fits around fasting temozolomide and meals for capecitabine. Follow the local rescue and constipation/diarrhoea plan.

Keep each medicine in its own labelled original packaging and away from children. Do not cut or crush capecitabine or open temozolomide capsules. If swallowing is difficult, contact pharmacy before treatment. Return unused medicine as advised.

regimen_profiles.regimen_role: Progressive, unresectable or metastatic, well-differentiated G1/G2 somatostatin-receptor-positive gastroenteropancreatic NET under NCCP 00642a.
regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: PRRT carries radiation to somatostatin receptors on NET cells to help control disease that cannot be removed or has spread. A specialist NET and nuclear-medicine team checks receptor imaging, organ function and your priorities before recommending it.
regimen_profiles.treatment_setting: Progressive, unresectable or metastatic, well-differentiated G1/G2 somatostatin-receptor-positive gastroenteropancreatic NET under NCCP 00642a.
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Lutetium-177 oxodotreotide: Lutathera joins a receptor-binding molecule to the radioactive element lutetium-177. After infusion, it attaches to somatostatin receptors on suitable NET cells and delivers radiation nearby. The receptor scan helps select patients. Kidneys and blood-forming marrow can also receive radiation, which is why kidney protection and long-term blood monitoring matter. Lysine / arginine amino acids: The amino-acid infusion reduces the amount of radioactive medicine retained in the kidneys. It is an essential part of kidney protection. It can cause nausea and affect potassium or fluid balance, so anti-sickness treatment, blood tests and observation are needed.
regimen_profiles.schedule_context: Four administrations are planned, usually eight weeks apart. Lutathera is infused over about 30–40 minutes, with a four-hour kidney-protective amino-acid infusion and anti-sickness treatment. The visit is much longer than the Lutathera infusion; an overnight stay may be needed.
key_points: Four administrations are planned, usually eight weeks apart. Lutathera is infused over about 30–40 minutes, with a four-hour kidney-protective amino-acid infusion and anti-sickness treatment. The visit is much longer than the Lutathera infusion; an overnight stay may be needed.

Baseline blood count, kidneys/liver, ECHO/MUGA and pregnancy assessment where applicable. Potassium is checked before amino acids. Renal monitoring continues at least through the first year. Post-infusion radiation scans and response scans have separate purposes.

Lutathera runs over approximately 30–40 minutes. A lysine/arginine amino-acid infusion starts 30 minutes beforehand and continues for four hours. The NET and nuclear-medicine teams must coordinate the injection plan. Do not translate “about four weeks” into your own date: NCCP specifies 30 days for long-acting SSA and 24 hours for short-acting SSA before PRRT. Restart timing follows the written service plan; it can differ with day-case arrangements.

Follow individual instructions on distance and time with other people, sleeping arrangements, toilets, body fluids, laundry, work and transport. Restrictions may extend to three weeks for some contacts. Contact the medical physicist before discharge if you cannot follow the plan at home.

Carry the discharge letter and treatment card, including the date and type of radioactive treatment. Ask about travel and radiation detectors. Tell any healthcare staff you have had PRRT; urgent care must never be delayed because of radiation precautions.

Lutathera can harm an unborn child and may affect fertility. Discuss fertility preservation before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for seven months after the last dose for patients who could become pregnant; men with partners who could become pregnant need contraception during treatment and for four months afterwards. Breastfeeding must stop before treatment; follow specialist advice.

The team decides whether a delayed administration remains suitable and whether activity must change. Do not assume a treatment can automatically proceed at the maximum interval. Continue the blood-test and symptom plan.

Write the actual NET, PRRT nursing and radiation-protection contacts on the paper plan. Example numbers are not clinical contact lines. Keep the written precautions and urgent hormone-symptom instructions with the discharge letter.

The detailed Irish leaflet describes three radiation-assessment scans on separate days in the first week after the first infusion, starting the next day, and one scan after later infusions. It also describes CT or MRI between the second and third infusions and after the course. These are service arrangements to confirm on your appointment sheet, not a universal timetable for every NET.

NCCP specifies four-weekly blood tests for at least three months, then three-monthly for the following year. The Irish service leaflet also describes fortnightly tests for eight weeks immediately after the final infusion. Your written discharge plan may therefore require more frequent early tests; follow that plan and ask the service to resolve any mismatch.

Before discharge, obtain a paper copy with the exact end date for each restriction. The Irish leaflet includes daily bathing, careful handwashing, sitting to pass urine and separate washing of body-fluid-soiled laundry in the first week. Ask for specific handling instructions for pads, incontinence or a catheter. Sleeping, travel, work and contact limits differ: examples include separate beds from a partner for 14 days and sleeping apart from pregnant people or children for three weeks. Your medical physicist’s personal instructions take precedence.

The medical physicist supplies a radiation-treatment card to carry for the time stated. The SACTCheck wallet card is an additional treatment record and does not replace that official card, the discharge letter or the radiation-safety plan.
